Passamaquoddy

Passamaquoddy/Peskotomuhkati includes distinct communities across the present Maine–New Brunswick border. This path prioritizes Sipayik’s community and language accounts and compares them with outside Saint Croix Island historical interpretation. A broad people label should not erase the differences among communities and institutions.

Read the sources [3] Sipayik Tribal Government [5] National Park Service, Saint Croix Island International Historic Site

01

Identity and context

Passamaquoddy communities have homelands across the modern U.S.–Canada border.

Read the sources [1] Passamaquoddy Tribe at Indian Township

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Peskotomuhkati naming, language, Wabanaki relationships and distinct communities. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] Passamaquoddy Tribe at Indian Township [2] legislature.maine.gov

03

Find separately named communities

Sipayik’s overview names Pleasant Point, Indian Township and a New Brunswick community separately, while emphasizing continuing relationships. It also describes Sipayik’s coastal fishing setting. This is one government’s account of community connections, not an independent determination that all communities share one present government or legal status.

Read the sources [3] Sipayik Tribal Government

04

Read language resources with their dates in mind

The Sipayik language account describes dictionary-making, school teaching and multimedia projects. Some passages refer to an envisioned CD-ROM and an unpublished digital version. Those legacy descriptions should guide further checking rather than be repeated as current software availability, speaker totals or proven teaching outcomes.

Read the sources [4] Sipayik Tribal Government

05

Compare perspectives on Saint Croix Island

National Park Service interpretation recounts the 1604–1605 French settlement and Passamaquoddy assistance after a difficult winter. It supplies context for the island photograph. Read this outside historical account alongside community publications; its broader ecological and land-ownership generalizations are not adopted here.

Read the sources [5] National Park Service, Saint Croix Island International Historic Site

About The Passamaquoddy Tribe — Sipayik account of communities and coastal life ↗

The Sipayik government describes coastal fishing relationships and separately names Pleasant Point, Indian Township and a New Brunswick community. Its account provides a route into distinct communities rather than one undifferentiated present government.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual About body lines249–254 and263: selected coastal resources, Sipayik fishing-village context, historical adaptation and explicitly named communities.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual selected public ordinary web-reader body independently read by the drafting researcher on 2026-10-28. No access bypass, outreach or automatic permission for linked media. Glacial/occupancy numbers, citizenship totals, ecological superlatives and present legal status/authority of every named community are not independently verified. Linked dictionary, history videos, photos and community websites were not automatically inspected.

History & Culture — selected Saint Croix Island historical interpretation ↗

The park’s interpretation places Saint Croix Island within Passamaquoddy history and recounts the 1604–1605 French settlement and Passamaquoddy assistance. It is an outside public-history account to compare with community publications.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual selected body lines26–38: island/community connection; seasonal river/coast context; French settlement, trade, difficult winter and assistance account.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual selected public ordinary web-reader body independently read by the drafting researcher on 2026-10-28. No access bypass, outreach or automatic permission for linked media. Numerical mortality/ecological totals, broad claims that Indigenous people did not own land, legal conclusions, universal harmony and first-contact absolutes are not adopted. Original journals, archaeology, sculptures, photos and linked collections uninspected.
